newsitem.title: GERMANY: Markets watchdog defends German insider rules.
newsitem.headline: Markets watchdog defends German insider rules.

text.p: The head of Germany's securities watchdog, the BAWe, sought to distance himself on Wednesday from an impression conveyed in a newspaper article that German insider trading laws are not completely strict.

BAWe President Georg Wittich had been quoted in the Handelsblatt newspaper as saying certain uses of privileged market information may not be illegal -- which the paper interpreted as giving a green light to insider dealing.
But Wittich told a university audience late on Wednesday that German laws banning insider dealing, which have only been in force since mid-1994, were as stiff as those in place elsewhere.
"German law is consistent with other European and international standards," he said.
Wittich reiterated that among the decisive factors in deciding whether to punish insider trading was the degree of impact the transactions had on the price of the stock involved.
"But one cannot deduce from this that insider trading is allowed," he said.
Earlier, Werner Seifert, head of the German Stock Exchange, told a news conference the BAWe president had been misinterpreted.

"That is not the Wittich we know," he said, adding that the BAWe and local stock market supervisors would continue to examine all transactions conducted on German exchanges and would follow up any suspicion of insider dealing.
The two-year-old BAWe's central task is eliminating insider trading in Germany.

The agency monitors hundreds of thousands of transactions daily to catch any aberrations, has investigated dozens of cases of suspected insider deals and has been instrumental in Germany's first ever prosecutions for such offences.
Current German securities law allows penalties of up to five years in jail for insider trading and jail terms have been so far imposed in two of the seven cases completed.
In the interview with Handelsblatt, Wittich said: "If the price move (of a stock) remains below the threshold of what might be termed considerable, then it is not an insider trade."
He also said that a price change would only be regarded as "considerable" if it exceeded "the normal fluctuation band."
On Wednesday evening, Wittich said it was difficult to set fixed parameters for determining normal fluctuations, since these differed from one stock to the next.
"These (suspected insider transactions) can only be dealt with on a case by case basis," he said.

A piece of insider information is described in German law as "every fact that is not yet publicly known .... which is capable of having a considerable effect on the price of the insider security, should it be announced publicly."
